meta.title: Hausa Alphabet (Boko)
meta.subtitle: 36 letters and sounds · both directions, as two cards per letter
meta.desc: The Latin alphabet in which Hausa is written (Boko): 36 notes, one per letter, in the order Nigerian primers give it, then the glottal stop, the rolled r that dictionaries mark r̃, the two diphthongs (ai, au) and the four digraphs with w and y (kw, gw, ƙw, ky). The first deck of the Hausa collection. Both directions: see a letter and recall its sound, or see a sound and recall the letter, each a card with its own schedule. Most of the letters sound as an English reader expects, and the cards say so in a line; the notes that matter are the ones English has no letter for — the IMPLOSIVES ɓ and ɗ, said with the air drawn slightly inward; the EJECTIVES ƙ and ts, said with the throat shut and a puff of air pushed out; the glottalised 'y (written ƴ in Niger); c, which is always the ch of church; and the apostrophe, which is a consonant. Each card gives one everyday word that shows the sound, from the Hausa A1 deck, with the same word beneath it with its tones and vowel length marked as English Wiktionary gives them (a grave accent for a low tone, a circumflex for a falling one, a macron for a long vowel; a high tone is unmarked) — marks that ordinary writing leaves out. The sounds are approximations, as every learner's alphabet gives them, for Standard (Kano) Hausa. There is no read-aloud button: few devices carry a Hausa voice, and one without it reads the letter in English. Sources: the standard description of Standard Hausa; the example words' tones are English Wiktionary's, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0).

fields.Sound: a vowel said long as the a of father, or short, close to the u of cut — writing does not show which
b, as in English
an IMPLOSIVE b: the voice box drops as the lips part, so the air is drawn slightly inward — a hollow, gulping b, a different sound from plain b
always the ch of church — never the c of cat or city
d, as in English
an IMPLOSIVE d: like ɓ, made with the voice box dropping and the air drawn slightly inward — a different sound from plain d
a pure vowel like the e of café, long or short, without the glide into "ee" of English day
an f made with both lips, as in blowing out a candle; many speakers say an English f, and some a p
always the hard g of go — never the g of gem
h, as in English
a vowel said long as the ee of see, or short as the i of bit
the j of jam
k, as in English
an EJECTIVE k: the throat is shut and a puff of air is pushed out with the k, giving a sharp popping k, a different sound from plain k
l, as in English
m, as in English
n, as in English; at the end of a syllable it takes the sound of the next consonant, and at the end of a word it can sound like the ng of sing
a pure vowel like the o of so, long or short, without the glide into "oo"
usually a FLAP made with the tongue tip curled back and flicked forward, close to the tt of American butter; ordinary writing does not tell it from the rolled r (r̃, below)
s, as in English — never the z sound of rose
the sh of shop; one sound, written with two letters
t, as in English
an EJECTIVE s (or ts): said with the throat shut and a puff of air pushed out, a hard hissing sound with a catch in it — one sound, not t followed by s
a vowel said long as the oo of food, or short as the u of put
w, as in English
the y of yes
a GLOTTALISED y: a y with a catch in the throat; written 'y in Nigeria and ƴ in Niger, the same letter
z, as in English; some speakers say it close to the j of jam before i and e

the apostrophe is a letter: a GLOTTAL STOP, the catch in the middle of uh-oh; it is written inside a word (sa'a) and left unwritten at the start of one, where every Hausa word that seems to begin with a vowel has it
the ROLLED r, a trill or tap of the tongue tip like a Spanish or Scottish r; ordinary writing spells it r, and only dictionaries mark it r̃, as the tone lines in these decks do
a diphthong like the i of kite; in Kano speech often nearer the ay of say
a diphthong like the ow of cow; in Kano speech often nearer the o of so
k with rounded lips, as in the qu of queen — one sound, with gw and ƙw beside it
